texts.e31c5921bc79:
Objective for processing:  
Babies who were born premature may suffer many adversities after birth. As they grow up, some are at risk of problems relating to health, cognition and behaviour, while others are resilient. These differences may be related to different and identifiable neurodevelopmental trajectories, the life-long process by which the brain grows and adapts to change.
In 1979–84, 224 infants who were born at less than 33 weeks of gestation and were admitted to the Neonatal Unit at University College London Hospital (UCLH) were enrolled by their parents into a longitudinal follow-up study investigating the developmental consequences of very premature birth. 
The cohort was seen at various points throughout their life including 1, 4, 14, 18 and 21 years. The cohort is now being brought back for a further follow-up at age 30. This study is supported by the Medical Research Council (ref: MR/K004867/1). 
First, their cognition and mental health will be assessed, with the hypothesis that many of these individuals may be “suffering in silence” with difficulties which are not of a sufficient threshold to have come to the attention of the medical profession but which still cause substantial problems in adulthood.
Second, various neuroimaging techniques will be used to examine how the brains of individuals born very prematurely change as they grow into adults. The principal aim of the study will be to define for the first time the patterns of brain growth that make a person born very prematurely at risk of cognitive and psychological problems, as well as those that are associated with resilience. In the future, this information will enable the development of treatments to reduce or prevent long-term disability in people born very prematurely.
In the intervening 10-15 years since study participants last took part, a proportion of the contact details have become out-of-date and assistance is required in tracking down these individuals to see if they are still willing to participate in this stage of the study. For those individuals who were assessed when they were 18 or over, the applicant has consent forms. All individuals who agree to take part in this stage of the follow-up will be reconsented.
Processing activities:
King's College London (KCL)  have full names and dates of birth for the individuals from the original cohort of 224 who they have not been able to contact for this follow-up. 
KCL will provide the HSCIC with this data and receive back current contact details (i.e. addresses) as well as their GP details. 
KCL will store this information in an encrypted and secure format at KCL and only the Data Controller and Data Processor will have access to it. 
The Data Processor will write to these individuals explaining the current follow-up study and asking them if they wish to take part, in a similar manner to contact which has been made with those who they do have current contact details for. In the initial contact letter KCL will include, besides the study protocol and consent sheet, a slip they can return which will give them the option of: 
a)	asking not to be contacted again for any future follow-up or
b)	an expression of interest in future follow-up studies but no interest in taking part in this particular study. 
In the case of response a, KCL will delete all information (e.g. name, d.o.b., next-of-kin information) from their databases and not contact them again in the future. In the case of response b, they will be asked if the applicants can contact them at regular intervals, such as yearly, by letter/email/phone in order that they can keep in touch with them and not need to utilise the HSCIC in the future to regain contact.
No record-level data is being provided to any 3rd parties. Only aggregated and fully anonymised data will be published in scientific journals or presented at Academic conferences (see below for further details).
Specific outputs expected, including target date:
The remaining individuals from the original cohort who can be contacted via the HSCIC and who wish to participate in this stage of the follow-up will be invited to take part and will provide neuropscyhological and brain imaging data (via MRI) which will be analyzed and published (anonymously) in international peer-reviewed journals and disseminated at conferences. 
Previous data from earlier follow-ups with this cohort have been published in high-impact scientific journals such as ‘Pediatrics’ (see ‘Preterm birth and adolescent social functioning-alterations in emotion-processing brain areas’, Pediatrics, 2013, Vol. 163(6): 1596-604.) as well as presented at international scientific conferences such as the Pediatric Academic Societies conference in Vancouver in 2014. The gradual accumulation of knowledge and understanding of the long-term sequale of preterm birth which will be afforded by these endeavours are absolutely crucial in improving the treatment and care of preterm birth survivors in the coming decades.
No 3rd parties will receive any data. Data published in scientific journals or presented at academic conferences will be aggregated and fully anonymised, in line with the HES analysis guide.
Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care including target date:
Premature birth is a major public health problem, costing the UK in excess of £900 million a year in neonatal medical care and subsequent monitoring, care and rehabilitative therapy. 
The study of brain maturation into adulthood following very preterm birth will enable the KCL to identify the mechanisms underlying the variations in adult outcomes and thus recognize subgroups of individuals who are at an increased risk of long-lasting neurodevelopmental problems and who could be prospectively identified and closely monitored - to decide if, when and what interventions may be appropriate.
The study could guide the development of remediation strategies to be implemented at younger ages, aimed at attenuating or even preventing long-term disability, thus improving the quality of life of very preterm individuals and shaping and enhancing the effectiveness of public services (for instance, preventing academic difficulties in preterm children using adaptive cognitive intervention programs).
Furthermore, the results of this study could be clinically important in leading to a greater understanding of the link between the brain developmental patterns seen in premature birth and the increased vulnerability of these individuals to develop psychiatric disorders. Recent research in individuals with an ‘at risk mental state’ suggests that the initiation of treatment before the onset of a psychiatric disorder (e.g., psychosis) may prevent or delay the development of the disorder. Therefore, in the medium term, the research could have an impact on the care management of preterm populations, as described in various policies and care pathways, as well as informing the work of carers, therapists, and charities/associations that provide help and support and campaign for those with neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., British Neuroscience Association).
